title: CBrio: growing knowledge from chemical gardens
content:
“If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need.”

This famous quote by Cicero reminds us that the beauty of life lies in the harmony between nature and knowledge. More than two thousand years later, this idea still resonates, particularly with a group of European researchers who have created a unique type of ‘garden’: one that grows from chemistry itself.

When certain metal salts are placed in water, strange, delicate, plant-like tubes and filaments begin to grow, twisting and blooming into colourful shapes. These creations, known as chemical gardens, are the result of natural chemical reactions. What appears to be art is actually science in motion.

Behind these mesmerising shapes lies a complex world of physics, chemistry and biology. Understanding these reactions could help scientists to design new materials, improve biomedical devices, capture gases such as carbon dioxide and even gain insight into how life first emerged on Earth.
snippet: “If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need.”

title: From conference grant to career milestone: the journey to an Early Career Research Award
content:
In July 2026, Vancouver, Canada hosted the 10th World Congress of Biomechanics (WCB26), the world’s leading congress on biomechanics and mechanobiology, organised every four years. This edition has been jointly organised by the European Society of Biomechanics, the American Society of Biomechanics and the Canadian Society of Biomechanics. WCB provides the latest research outputs on biomechanics and brings together researchers and scientists expert in wearable sensors, artificial intelligence, regenerative medicine, and novel devices, to name a few.

ESB awards promote excellence in biomechanics research to foster integration of clinical and basic science, and to facilitate the translation of that science to health care and clinical practice.

The ESB Early Career Research Award, initiated in 2023, recognises the development of an outstanding young researcher in the process of career consolidation, who contributes to the advancement of the theory and/or applications of Biomechanics and/or mechanobiology.

title: Short visits, lasting impact – How COST Short-Term Scientific Missions shape research journeys
content:
More than 2000+ Short-Term Scientific Missions (STSM) are funded yearly by COST. Open to researchers at all career stages, STSMs are one of COST’s most impactful networking tools. These scientific missions allow researchers involved in a COST Action to visit a university, a research institute or laboratory in another country to collaborate, access expertise and research infrastructure that may not be available at their home institution. 

Although these missions are called “short-term”, their impact often extends well beyond the exchange.  The Impact Assessment Study on Short-Term Mobility found that STSMs contribute to higher-quality research, developed skills, and new research collaborations, projects and proposals. Many STSMs also lead to joint publications between the visiting researcher and the host, or even common European or national research proposals. STSMs provide a good opportunity for both young and experienced researchers looking for mentoring and lifelong learning while helping institutions and COST Actions strengthen their networks, foster collaboration, and develop new scientific outputs.

title: EUGAIN: closing the gap in informatics
content:
The algorithms, apps, and software that shape our daily lives are predominantly designed by men. Despite the sector’s explosive growth, women remain a small minority among informatics students, researchers, and professors. And this gap has barely moved in decades.

When so few women are involved in designing, building, and leading in computing, the technologies that support our lives only reflect one part of society. These technologies are blind to the needs and risks that a more diverse public would identify.

Closing the gender gap requires more than just encouraging girls to learn to code. Universities, companies and policymakers must rethink how they teach, recruit and support people at every stage of their careers.

This was the starting point for the COST Action European Network for Gender Balance in Informatics (EUGAIN). Its initiators noticed that many universities already had isolated initiatives addressing gender balance, but no one was connecting the people behind them. title: EuroWeb: From Ancient Threads to Digital Platforms
content:
Every piece of fabric has a story to tell. The colours, patterns and weaves of each piece reveal centuries of craft, trade and cultural exchange. Some of these stories are hidden in the mineralised textiles of Pompeii, while others lie in the ancient silk routes that once connected Asia and Europe, or in the wool and dyes that clothed everyone from kings to ordinary people.

The COST Action Europe Through Textiles: Network for an integrated and interdisciplinary Humanities (EuroWeb) connected people studying these stories. From archaeologists and conservators to fashion historians and textile artists, EuroWeb created a network where knowledge could travel as freely as fabrics once did.

title: Science communication best practice: CosmoVerse
content:
By observing the universe, we can compare our theories with the facts. Yet reconciling theoretical expectations with reality has become increasingly challenging, as different measurements of the same quantity often yield conflicting results, much like two builders disagreeing on a door’s size. If similar discrepancies emerge in other measurements, the integrity of the entire framework could be called into question.

The growing discrepancies between measurements obtained by different teams are creating significant tensions within the current cosmological model and call for a concerted effort to uncover their origin. Are these differences rooted in the way observational data are collected? Do they arise from the methods used to analyse the data? Or do they point to limitations in the theoretical framework employed to interpret the observations?

title: PROGRAMMING: growing older better
content:
Europe is getting older. People are living longer than ever before, but a longer life does not always mean a healthier life. Chronic illness and disability often come with ageing, creating a burden not only for families but also for healthcare systems and society.

Recognising this, the World Health Organisation launched the Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030), calling for global action to improve the lives of older people around the world.

The challenge is not simply helping people live longer, but helping them live better. According to studies, a large part of poor quality of life in later years can be prevented or delayed with the right care at the right time.

This is where geriatric medicine becomes essential. Unlike traditional medical approaches that often focus on a single disease, geriatric medicine looks at the person’s physical health, mental well-being, daily functioning, medications, and social environment.

title: COST Action blog: FruitCREWS concludes at the European Parliament with a Call for Water Resilience
content:
Written by COST Action FruitCREWS in Brussels on 24 June 2026

More than four years of collaborative research, knowledge exchange and stakeholder engagement culminated this week as the COST Action FruitCREWS (Fruit tree Crop REsponses to Water deficit and decision support Systems applications) held its final workshop at the European Parliament Info Hub, in a Brussels hit by an unprecedent heat wave: the perfect context for reminding us of the strong consequences of climate change on both the population and on EU agriculture.
